sections.title: From Zero to Book 5
sections.body: Book 5 assumes you've worked through books 1-4: the core particles, verb conjugations, and everyday vocabulary from those books are used freely here without re-explanation. What's new in book 5 is depth — grammar patterns get more nuanced, sentences get longer, and kanji moves from 'nice to recognize' to 'expected to read.' If a sentence feels dense at first, that's normal at this level: read it once for the grammar pattern, then again for the vocabulary. Progress from here is less about learning brand-new basics and more about noticing the small differences between similar-sounding grammar — which is exactly what this book focuses on.

points.title: Direct translation (直訳) vs natural translation (意訳)
points.explanation: A word-for-word (直訳) rendering of a Japanese sentence often reads as stiff or even confusing in English, and the reverse is just as true. From here on, translations in this book favor what a native speaker would actually say (意訳) over a literal word match. That means some words appear to 'vanish' or 'appear' in translation — that's expected, not a mistake.

examples.japanese: お風呂をいれたよ。
examples.romaji: Ofuro wo iretayo. (lit. "I put in the bath")
examples.english: I drew a bath.

examples.romaji: Isogashikute, te ga mawaranai. (lit. "my hands don't reach around")

points.title: Advanced grammar isn't automatically 'better' grammar
points.explanation: A nuanced, high-level grammar pattern is not a fancier replacement for a simpler one — each has its own register and situations where it's actually used. Reach for the grammar that matches the situation and the feeling you want to convey, not the most advanced one you know.

points.title: Grammar and vocabulary depend on each other
points.explanation: Grammar without vocabulary produces empty sentence shapes; vocabulary without grammar produces a word list, not a sentence. From this point on, both are drilled together rather than in isolation — new grammar patterns are practiced immediately with the new vocabulary from the same lesson.

sections.title: Why this lesson exists
sections.body: Book 5 assumes you can already read a set of common kanji that sits right at the boundary between books 4 and 5. This lesson is a bridge: 40 kanji grouped by theme (descriptive words, the body, family members, common verbs, communication verbs, and plants & animals) that you'll see used freely from Lesson 1 onward. If any of these are new to you, spend a little extra time here before moving on.

points.title: 何とか + verb (to handle/manage something)
points.explanation: 何とか paired with a verb means you'll manage to get something done somehow, even without a clear plan for how. It shows up constantly in casual conversation as a way to sound reassuring without promising specifics.

examples.japanese: 何とかなります。
examples.english: It'll work out somehow.

examples.japanese: 何とか時間をつくります。
examples.english: I'll manage to make time somehow.

points.title: 〜のに with verbs and い-adjectives (even though)
points.explanation: のに attaches directly to the plain form of a verb or い-adjective to mean 'even though.' Unlike から or ので, のに often carries a hint of surprise, frustration, or unmet expectation.

examples.japanese: 忙しいのに、てつだってくれた。
examples.english: Even though he was busy, he helped me out.

examples.japanese: 勉強したのに、わすれた。
examples.english: Even though I studied, I forgot.

points.title: 〜のに with nouns and な-adjectives (even though)
points.explanation: With nouns and な-adjectives, な is inserted before のに, exactly like it is before other な-adjective connectors.

examples.japanese: しずかなのに、ねむれない。
examples.english: Even though it's quiet, I can't sleep.

examples.japanese: 休みなのに、はたらいている。
examples.english: Even though it's a day off, he's working.

points.title: 〜てみる (trying something out)
points.explanation: Attaching てみる to a verb frames the action as an experiment — you're trying it to see what happens, not necessarily committing to it long-term.

examples.japanese: たべてみます。
examples.english: I'll try eating it.

examples.japanese: 新しいアプリをつかってみた。
examples.english: I tried using a new app.

points.title: Verb + 〜たりしますか (Do you ever...?)
points.explanation: The 〜たり form followed by します turns a single verb into a casual 'do you ever (do this, among other things)?' question — it softens the question and implies it's just one example among several possible activities.

examples.japanese: ひとりで映画にいったりしますか。
examples.romaji: Hitori de eiga ni ittari shimasu ka.
examples.english: Do you ever go to the movies alone?

examples.japanese: 週末は本をよんだり、テレビをみたりします。
examples.romaji: Shuumatsu wa hon wo yondari, terebi wo mitari shimasu.
examples.english: On weekends I do things like read books and watch TV.

points.title: Confirming a reason with 〜(な)んです
points.explanation: んです (informally) or なんです (after nouns/な-adjectives) frames a statement as an explanation the listener is expected to already sense the context for — it adds a confirming, 'that's why' tone that plain です doesn't carry.

examples.japanese: 風邪をひいたんです。
examples.english: (That's why) I caught a cold.

examples.japanese: 今日は休みなんです。
examples.english: (You see,) today is a day off.

points.title: 〜(な)んです for emphasis
points.explanation: The same construction can shift from 'explaining' to simply emphasizing a fact, especially in response to a surprised reaction from the listener.

examples.japanese: 本当に大きくなったんです。
examples.english: You've really gotten big!

examples.japanese: このかばん、たかかったんです。
examples.english: This bag, it was expensive, you know.

points.title: 〜(な)んです vs から
points.explanation: から states a reason directly and can sound abrupt on its own; んです frames the same content as background explanation, which reads as softer and more natural in conversation.

examples.japanese: 寒いから、窓をしめた。
examples.english: Because it's cold, I closed the window.

examples.japanese: 寒いんです。窓、しめてもいいですか。
examples.romaji: Samui ndesu. Mado, shimete mo ii desu ka.
examples.english: It's cold (you see). Is it okay if I close the window?

points.title: 〜ながら (doing two things at once)
points.explanation: ながら attaches to a verb's ます-stem to show two actions happening simultaneously, with the ながら-marked verb being the secondary, background activity.

examples.japanese: 音楽をききながら勉強します。
examples.english: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: テレビをみながらご飯をたべた。
examples.romaji: Terebi wo minagara gohan wo tabeta.
examples.english: I ate dinner while watching TV.

points.title: Adding background information with が and けど
points.explanation: が and けど both loosely connect two clauses without necessarily meaning 'but' — often they just add context before the main point, similar to English 'so, anyway...'.

examples.japanese: 雨がふっていますが、でかけます。
examples.romaji: Ame ga futte imasu ga, dekakemasu.
examples.english: It's raining, but I'm heading out anyway.

points.title: 〜っぱなし (leaving something on/going; keeps doing)
points.explanation: っぱなし attaches to a verb's ます-stem to describe something left in an ongoing state, usually carelessly or without attention — a light left on, a door left open, or a habit kept up too long.

examples.japanese: 電気をつけっぱなしにした。
examples.english: I left the light on.

examples.japanese: ドアをあけっぱなしにしないでください。
examples.romaji: Doa wo akeppanashi ni shinaide kudasai.
examples.english: Please don't leave the door open.

points.title: Hearsay: 〜んだって / 〜って (I heard that...)
points.explanation: って (casual) tacked onto the end of a plain-form sentence reports something you heard from someone else, without vouching for it yourself — much lighter than という話です.

examples.japanese: 明日雨だって。
examples.english: I heard it's supposed to rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼、結婚するんだって。
examples.english: I heard he's getting married.

points.title: って used to ask 'what do you mean?'
points.explanation: The same って particle, placed right after a word someone just said, turns into a quick clarifying echo — 'the what now?'

examples.japanese: これ、むりょうですよ。— むりょうって？
examples.romaji: Kore, muryou desu yo. — Muryou tte?
examples.english: This is free. — Free, as in...?

examples.japanese: ちこくした。— ちこくって、何時に？
examples.romaji: Chikoku shita. — Chikoku tte, nanji ni?
examples.english: I was late. — Late, as in what time?

points.title: 〜がる with adjectives (what someone else feels)
points.explanation: い-adjectives that describe internal feelings (寒い, 嬉しい, 欲しい) can't be used directly about a third person's feelings in Japanese — がる converts them into a verb describing observed behavior instead.

examples.japanese: 妹は新しい靴をほしがっている。
examples.romaji: Imouto wa atarashii kutsu wo hoshigatte iru.
examples.english: My little sister wants new shoes.

examples.japanese: 子供はさむがっている。
examples.english: The child seems cold.

points.title: 〜がる with たい-form verbs
points.explanation: The same restriction applies to 〜たい (want to do) — for a third person, it becomes 〜たがる, describing the visible want rather than claiming to know their internal state directly.

examples.japanese: 彼は早くかえりたがっている。
examples.english: He seems eager to go home early.

examples.japanese: 息子は犬をかいたがっている。
examples.romaji: Musuko wa inu wo kaitagatte iru.
examples.english: My son seems to want to get a dog.

points.title: 〜がする (describing a sensory impression)
points.explanation: がする attaches after a sensory noun (匂い, 味, 音, 気) to describe a smell, taste, sound, or feeling you're perceiving, without needing a separate verb for each sense.

examples.japanese: いい匂いがする。
examples.english: It smells good.

examples.japanese: なんか嫌なかんじがする。
examples.romaji: Nanka iya na kanji ga suru.
examples.english: I've got a bad feeling about this.

sections.body: 北 (north) carries a secondary, almost superstitious association with defeat or retreat in some set phrases and idioms — likely tied to historical compass-direction symbolism where north was linked to withdrawal. It's a good reminder that direction kanji, like many kanji, pick up figurative meanings well beyond their literal one.

sections.body: Several Japanese idioms borrow nature kanji for emotional or social states — someone daydreaming or acting spacey can be described with cloud imagery, and a sudden run of bad luck sometimes gets described with a 'broken star' metaphor. points.title: 〜てしまう (carrying an action through to the end)
points.explanation: てしまう marks an action as completed all the way through, sometimes with a sense of finality or 'no going back now.'

points.title: 〜てしまう for unconscious or unintended actions
points.explanation: The same form frequently marks something that happened without the speaker meaning for it to — a slip, an accident, or a regret. Context (not different grammar) is what signals 'on purpose' vs 'oops' here.

points.title: 〜てしまう as a threat or statement of resolve
points.explanation: Less commonly, てしまう on a future action can sound like a firm intention or even a mild threat — 'I'm going to just do it (and there's nothing you can do about it).'

sections.title: Kanji Culture
sections.body: Many kanji share a 'phonetic component' — a piece that hints at the on'yomi reading rather than the meaning. 寺 (じ/てら) shows up inside 時 (とき/ジ) and 詩 (シ), and in each case that shared piece nudges the reading toward じ/シ. Spotting these recurring components can help you guess an unfamiliar kanji's reading before you look it up.

sections.title: Culture Clip
sections.body: The 河童 (kappa) is one of Japan's best-known yokai — a river-dwelling creature said to be equal parts cute and dangerous, often drawn with a dish of water on its head that's the source of its strength. Meanwhile, 相撲 (sumo) is considered Japan's oldest organized sport, with roots tied to Shinto ritual centuries before it became the spectator sport it is today.

points.title: 'A thing called...' / 'A place called...' (というもの / というところ)
points.explanation: というもの and というところ introduce an unfamiliar item or place by name before explaining what it is — useful for defining new concepts to a listener.

points.explanation: はじめる attaches to a verb's ます-stem to mark the start of an action, regardless of whether it's finished yet.

points.title: Passive verb form 〜られる / 〜れる
points.explanation: The passive form shifts focus onto the receiver of an action rather than the doer — in Japanese it's also frequently used for an 'adversity passive,' implying the speaker was inconvenienced by something happening to or around them.

points.title: Review: the volitional (よう) form
points.explanation: The volitional form (行こう, 食べよう) means 'let's' or 'I shall' on its own — this lesson builds directly on it, so a quick refresher first: it's formed by shifting a verb's final u-sound to its o-sound equivalent and adding う (godan verbs), or replacing る with よう (ichidan verbs).

examples.japanese: いこう。
examples.english: Let's go.

examples.japanese: たべよう。
examples.english: Let's eat.

points.title: 〜(よ)うとする (attempting to do something)
points.explanation: Volitional form + とする describes the moment of attempting an action — often used for something that was attempted but didn't quite succeed.

examples.japanese: ドアをあけようとしたが、あかなかった。
examples.romaji: Doa wo akeyou to shita ga, akanakatta.
examples.english: I tried to open the door, but it wouldn't open.

examples.japanese: 電車にのりおくれまいとして、はしった。
examples.romaji: Densha ni noriokuremai to shite, hashitta.
examples.english: I ran, trying not to miss the train.

points.title: 〜とたんに (the moment that...)
points.explanation: とたんに marks the instant one thing happens, immediately followed by a second, often surprising event.

examples.japanese: 家をでたとたんに、雨がふりだした。
examples.romaji: Ie wo deta totan ni, ame ga furidashita.
examples.english: The moment I left the house, it started raining.

examples.japanese: 彼の顔をみたとたんに、誰かわかった。
examples.romaji: Kare no kao wo mita totan ni, dare ka wakatta.
examples.english: The moment I saw his face, I knew who he was.

points.title: ため with nouns (for the sake of / because of)
points.explanation: Noun + の + ため carries two related senses: 'for the sake/benefit of' (positive) or 'because of' (neutral cause), disambiguated by context.

examples.japanese: 家族のためにはたらいています。
examples.romaji: Kazoku no tame ni hataraite imasu.
examples.english: I'm working for my family's sake.

points.title: ため with verbs (in order to / because)
points.explanation: The same ため attaches after a verb's plain form with the same two senses — purpose when the verb is deliberate, cause when it isn't.

examples.japanese: しけんにうかるために、勉強しています。
examples.romaji: Shiken ni ukaru tame ni, benkyou shite imasu.
examples.english: I'm studying in order to pass the exam.

points.title: 様態のそう: verb ます-stem/adjective stem + そう (looks like...)
points.explanation: Attached directly to a verb's ます-stem or an adjective's stem (dropping い), そう expresses a visual impression — 'it looks like...' based on what you're observing right now.

examples.japanese: 雨がふりそうです。
examples.english: It looks like it's about to rain.

examples.japanese: この犯人、うそをつきそうですね。
examples.romaji: Kono hannin, uso wo tsukisou desu ne.
examples.english: This suspect looks like they're about to lie, doesn't it.

points.title: そう about your own state
points.explanation: The same construction works for describing your own apparent state as it would look to someone else observing you.

examples.japanese: つかれそうな顔をしているね。
examples.romaji: Tsukaresou na kao wo shite iru ne.
examples.english: You look tired.

points.title: Negative assumptions: 〜そうにない / 〜なさそう
points.explanation: For 'doesn't look like it will happen,' verbs typically use 〜そうにない, while adjectives use 〜なさそう (dropping the negative い and adding さそう).

examples.japanese: 雨がやみそうにない。
examples.english: It doesn't look like the rain will stop.

examples.japanese: おいしくなさそう。
examples.english: It doesn't look tasty.

points.title: Verb/adjective + そう as a noun modifier
points.explanation: そう + な can modify a following noun directly, letting you describe a noun by how it appears rather than what it is.

examples.japanese: おいしそうなケーキですね。
examples.english: That looks like a delicious cake.

points.title: 伝聞のそうです: plain form + そうです (hearsay)
points.explanation: Unlike 様態のそう above, this そうです attaches to a full plain-form sentence and never conjugates — it reports something you heard, read, or were told, with no visual guessing involved.

examples.japanese: てんきよほうによると、明日は雨だそうです。
examples.romaji: Tenki yohou ni yoru to, ashita wa ame da sou desu.
examples.english: According to the forecast, it's supposed to rain tomorrow.

points.title: によると (according to)
points.explanation: によると introduces the source of the information that follows, almost always paired with hearsay そうです or らしい at the end of the sentence.

examples.japanese: ニュースによると、じこがあったそうです。
examples.romaji: Nyuusu ni yoru to, jiko ga atta sou desu.
examples.english: According to the news, there was an accident.

examples.japanese: 警察によると、犯人はもうつかまったそうです。
examples.romaji: Keisatsu ni yoru to, hannin wa mou tsukamatta sou desu.
examples.english: According to the police, the perpetrator has already been caught.

units.label: Lesson 10
units.title: ばかり and かもしれない

points.title: ばかり with a noun (nothing but...)
points.explanation: Noun + ばかり means 'nothing but that thing' — often with a mildly critical tone about an unbalanced habit.

examples.japanese: お菓子ばかりたべている。
examples.english: All he eats is snacks.

points.title: ばかり with a number (about, roughly)
points.explanation: After a quantity, ばかり softens it into an approximation, very close in feel to くらい/ぐらい.

examples.japanese: じゅっぷんばかりまちました。
examples.english: I waited for about ten minutes.

points.title: 〜てばかり (constantly/only doing)
points.explanation: Verb て-form + ばかり(いる) describes an ongoing habit the speaker views as excessive or one-sided — playing games all day, complaining nonstop, etc.

examples.japanese: 家でゲームをしてばかりいる。
examples.romaji: Ie de geemu wo shite bakari iru.
examples.english: All he does is play video games at home.

points.title: 〜たばかり (just finished doing)
points.explanation: Verb past-tense (た) + ばかり means the action was completed very recently — 'I just...'

examples.japanese: 今きたばかりです。
examples.english: I just got here.

examples.japanese: こくはくしたばかりです。
examples.english: I just confessed my feelings.

points.title: 〜かもしれない (might; there's a chance that)
points.explanation: かもしれない attaches to a plain-form clause to express a degree of uncertainty weaker than 'probably' — a genuine 'maybe.'

examples.japanese: 明日、会社をやすむかもしれない。
examples.english: I might take tomorrow off work.

examples.japanese: 電車にまにあわないかもしれない。
examples.romaji: Densha ni ma ni awanai kamoshirenai.
examples.english: I might not make it in time for the train.

points.title: 〜たらいいのに / 〜たらいい (I wish... / it'd be nice if...)
points.explanation: た-form + らいい(のに) expresses a wish for a hypothetical, often unlikely, situation — のに at the end adds a note of regret that it isn't actually the case.

examples.japanese: もっと時間があったらいいのに。
examples.romaji: Motto jikan ga attara ii noni.
examples.english: I wish I had more time.

points.title: つもり with verbs (intending to)
points.explanation: Plain-form verb + つもり states a personal intention — a plan you hold in your head, not necessarily one that's been announced or finalized.

examples.japanese: 来月、日本にいくつもりです。
examples.romaji: Raigetsu, Nihon ni iku tsumori desu.
examples.english: I'm planning to go to Japan next month.

points.title: つもり for a mistaken belief
points.explanation: つもり can also describe believing something about yourself (often false, per the listener's perspective) — 'I think of myself as...' even when others would disagree.

examples.japanese: まだ若いつもりです。
examples.english: I still think of myself as young.

points.title: というのは (beginning an explanation)
points.explanation: というのは opens an explanation of a reason or definition just given, functioning much like English 'that is to say...' or 'the reason is...'

examples.japanese: やすみます。というのは、たいちょうがわるいからです。
examples.romaji: Yasumimasu. To iu no wa, taichou ga warui kara desu.
examples.english: I'll be off. The reason is, I'm not feeling well.

examples.japanese: 秘密にしたい。というのは、まだ完璧じゃないからです。
examples.romaji: Himitsu ni shitai. To iu no wa, mada kanpeki ja nai kara desu.
examples.english: I want to keep it a secret. The reason is, it's not perfect yet.

points.title: かというと with question words
points.explanation: Question word + かというと sets up 'as for [what/who/where]...' before answering your own implied question — a natural way to preview a specific answer.

examples.japanese: どこにいきたいかというと、おきなわです。
examples.romaji: Doko ni ikitai ka to iu to, Okinawa desu.
examples.english: As for where I want to go, it's Okinawa.

points.title: かというと across different tenses
points.explanation: The same structure works fine in past or negative form on either side — the question-word clause and the answer clause tense independently.

examples.japanese: なぜいかなかったかというと、いそがしかったからです。
examples.romaji: Naze ikanakatta ka to iu to, isogashikatta kara desu.
examples.english: As for why I didn't go, it's because I was busy.

points.title: うち (within a span; while it's still...)
points.explanation: うち marks a window of time you want to act within before it closes — 'while it's still...', 'before it stops being true.'

examples.japanese: 暖かいうちにたべてください。
examples.english: Please eat it while it's still warm.

points.title: 〜だらけ (covered in; full of, usually negative)
points.explanation: だらけ attaches to a noun to mean 'covered in/riddled with' — almost always something undesirable (mistakes, dust, debt).

examples.japanese: このレポートはまちがいだらけです。
examples.romaji: Kono repooto wa machigai darake desu.
examples.english: This report is riddled with mistakes.

points.title: More verb-derived nouns
points.explanation: Beyond simple ます-stem nouns, some verb-derived nouns shift slightly in form or meaning (話 from 話す, 帰り from 帰る) — worth learning case by case rather than as a strict rule.

examples.japanese: かえりにストアによります。
examples.english: I'll stop by the store on the way home.

sections.title: Kanji Culture
sections.body: The verb はかる ('to measure/plan') has at least four different kanji depending on what's being measured: 計る (time, quantity in general), 測る (length, depth, speed), 量る (weight, volume), and 図る (scheming or planning something abstract). Native speakers pick the right one by what's actually being measured — a good reminder that one English gloss can hide several distinct kanji.

points.title: Causative 〜させる (making/letting someone do)
points.explanation: The causative form covers both 'make someone do' and 'let someone do,' with the specific reading decided by context and particle choice rather than the verb form itself.

examples.japanese: 子供に部屋をかたづけさせた。
examples.english: I made my child tidy their room.

points.title: Particle choice with させる: を vs に
points.explanation: With an intransitive verb, the causee takes を; with a transitive verb (which already has its own を-marked object), the causee shifts to に instead to avoid stacking two を's.

examples.japanese: 子供をはしらせた。
examples.english: I made the child run. (intransitive: 走る)

examples.japanese: 子供に本をよませた。
examples.english: I had the child read the book. (transitive: 読む)

points.title: Quick review: causative vs passive vs causative-passive
points.explanation: It's worth keeping させる (causative: make/let do), られる (passive: have done to oneself), and させられる (causative-passive: forced to do, against one's will) clearly separated, since their forms are easy to mix up under pressure.

points.title: Why you can't mark two things with を in one clause
points.explanation: Because を marks a direct object, a clause can only carry one — this is exactly why the causee's particle has to switch to に whenever the base verb already has its own direct object.

points.title: させてください (please let me do)
points.explanation: させる + てください politely requests permission to do something yourself — a common, natural way to ask for the floor, a turn, or a chance to help.

examples.japanese: 私にやらせてください。
examples.english: Please let me do it.

points.title: Double particles review
points.explanation: Combining causative/passive forms with things like ておく or てもらう can stack particles in ways that look unfamiliar at first — read them from the innermost verb outward to untangle the meaning.

examples.japanese: 親にてつだわせてもらった。
examples.english: I had my parent let me help.

sections.title: Kanji Culture
sections.body: 形 is the go-to suffix for naming shapes: 三角形 (triangle, 'three-corner shape'), 四角形 (quadrilateral, 'four-corner shape'), 円形 (circle, 'round shape'). Once you know 形, most shape vocabulary becomes a simple number/adjective + 形 combination rather than a separate word to memorize for each one.

points.title: に: Japanese's hardest-working particle
points.explanation: に covers an unusually wide range of jobs — destination, time, indirect object, purpose, and more — which is exactly why it resists a single English translation. Context, not the particle itself, tells you which job it's doing.

examples.japanese: 会社にいきます。
examples.english: I'm going to the company. (destination)

points.title: に translating as 'for'
points.explanation: One of に's jobs is marking purpose or intended use — in this role it often reads best in English as 'for.'

examples.japanese: このはさみは紙を切るのにつかいます。
examples.romaji: Kono hasami wa kami wo kiru no ni tsukaimasu.
examples.english: These scissors are used for cutting paper.

points.title: のに that doesn't mean 'even though' (purpose のに)
points.explanation: の (nominalizer) + に (purpose particle from 13-2) can look identical to the 'even though' のに from Lesson 1 — this のに instead marks what a verb-phrase is used for.

examples.japanese: このアプリは日本語を勉強するのに便利です。
examples.romaji: Kono apuri wa Nihongo wo benkyou suru no ni benri desu.
examples.english: This app is convenient for studying Japanese.

points.title: Telling the two のに's apart
points.explanation: The purpose のに is followed by an adjective describing usefulness (便利, 役に立つ) and the whole の-clause acts like a noun; the 'even though' のに instead sits between two full clauses and signals contrast. When in doubt, check what comes right after のに.

points.title: Noun + でも (even if / even a...)
points.explanation: でも after a noun means 'even [that noun]' — extending an idea to an extreme or unlikely example to make a point.

examples.japanese: 子供でもできます。
examples.english: Even a child can do this.

examples.japanese: 十円玉でも、じはんきでかえます。
examples.romaji: Juuendama de mo, jihanki de kaemasu.
examples.english: You can even buy from the vending machine with just a 10-yen coin.

points.title: 〜ても with verbs (even if)
points.explanation: Verb て-form + も means 'even if' — the outcome in the second clause holds true regardless of the condition.

examples.japanese: 雨がふっても、いきます。
examples.english: Even if it rains, I'm going.

examples.japanese: 切符がきれても、えきいんにきけば大丈夫です。
examples.romaji: Kippu ga kirete mo, ekiin ni kikeba daijoubu desu.
examples.english: Even if your ticket expires, it's fine if you ask the station staff.

points.title: 〜ても with い-adjectives
points.explanation: For い-adjectives, drop the final い and add くても for the same 'even if' meaning.

examples.japanese: むずかしくても、がんばります。
examples.english: Even if it's difficult, I'll do my best.

examples.japanese: はずかしくても、お礼を言うべきです。
examples.romaji: Hazukashikute mo, orei wo iu beki desu.
examples.english: Even if it's embarrassing, you should say thank you.

points.title: Listing facts/conditions with 〜し〜し
points.explanation: し strings together multiple reasons or facts supporting the same conclusion, implying there are more that could be listed too.

examples.japanese: やすいし、おいしいし、またきます。
examples.english: It's cheap, it's delicious, I'll come again.

sections.title: Kanji Culture
sections.body: 室 shows up as a suffix across a huge range of room types: 教室 (classroom), 図書室 (library room), 会議室 (meeting room), 温室 (greenhouse). Learning 室 as a modular suffix, rather than memorizing each compound separately, makes new room-related vocabulary much easier to guess on sight.

同じ (おなじ) — same
一万 (いちまん) — ten thousand
日本刀 (にほんとう) — Japanese sword
図書室 (としょしつ) — library room
同時代 (どうじだい) — same era
万一 (まんいち) — just in case
何度 (なんど) — how many times
図書＿で勉強します。(I study in the library room.)
'What' (casual) is which kanji reading なに？

'Ten thousand' is which kanji?
